headline: Officials Confirm Airport Chaos Was Definitely Caused by Something
subheadline: *Nationwide ground stop traced to 'old hardware', a term of art meaning 'a machine, probably, from before'.*
author: Elsie Pemberton, Transport & Infrastructure Desk
seoTitle: Airport Chaos Definitely Caused by Something
seoDescription: Satire: US officials lifted the nationwide ground stop and confirmed the chaos was not a cyberattack or a Microsoft outage — just definitely caused by something.
sourceEvent: The United States lifted an hours-long nationwide ground stop on Friday, with officials stressing the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack or a sweeping Microsoft outage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy declared US airspace 'opened up' and blamed 'old hardware' for the chaos.

social.x: BREAKING: US officials confirm the nationwide ground stop was caused by neither hackers nor Microsoft, and would like everyone to please stop asking. Airspace 'opened up' thanks to hardware described only as 'old'. Full report:
social.facebook: America's entire aviation network was grounded for hours on Friday, and officials were quick to clarify what didn't cause it: hackers, Microsoft, a squirrel, or the moon. What DID cause it remains a proud national tradition of not asking follow-up questions about 'old hardware'.
social.linkedin: Friday's nationwide ground stop is a timely reminder that critical infrastructure runs on a strategic asset class known as 'old hardware'. Our full analysis of the resilience implications — none of which involve naming the hardware — below.
social.instagram: Good news: it wasn't hackers. Also good news: it wasn't Microsoft. Further news pending: what it actually was. Officials confirm the system runs on 'old hardware', which is a machine, probably, from before. #satire #aviation #groundstop #faa #travel
altHeadlines: Nation's Aviation Network Grounded by Router That Predates the Safety Videos
Officials Release Exhaustive List of 400 Things That Didn't Ground Every Plane in America

body:
WASHINGTON — The United States reopened its airspace on Friday after an hours-long nationwide ground stop, as federal officials moved swiftly to assure the public that the total shutdown of American aviation had been caused by neither a cyberattack nor a Microsoft outage — two of the roughly nine thousand possibilities it wasn't.

Transportation officials confirmed the disruption, which stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers and obliged airlines to reintroduce the concept of 'waiting', had been traced to 'old hardware', a technical term meaning a specific machine somewhere that everyone had politely agreed not to look at.

Officials announced that US airspace was now 'opened up', before spending the remainder of the press conference enumerating things the outage had definitely not been. The list, which expanded across the afternoon, eventually included hackers, foreign adversaries, a sweeping Microsoft failure, a localised Microsoft failure, a squirrel, the moon being in retrograde, and 'any software newer than the Bush administration — either Bush'.

'We want to be fully transparent with the American people,' said a spokesperson for the Department of Transportation. 'The system did exactly what it was designed to do, in the sense that it is old, and old things do this.'

Sources within the Federal Aviation Administration described the faulty component as a router acquired during a period when 'the cloud' referred to the weather affecting your flight, which is, in fairness, the cloud the system was protecting you from. Technicians reportedly restored service by unplugging the device, observing the traditional thirty seconds of silence, and blowing on it — a repair procedure appearing in no manual but ratified by international convention.

'People keep asking me what actually caused it,' said local man Dennis Barrow, 47, still seated in a departure lounge at an airport he declined to name. 'And the answer is: not that. Not that either. I've been here nine hours and I now know four hundred things it wasn't.'

Analysts praised the administration's commitment to ruling out explanations. 'Governments often rush to blame the wrong thing,' said one analyst. 'This administration took the bold step of blaming nothing, comprehensively, in alphabetical order.'

Aviation experts noted the national airspace runs on a patchwork of systems, several of which carry commemorative stickers from inaugurations most passengers were not alive for, and one of which is widely believed to be held together by a specific technician's emotional investment.

At press time, officials confirmed all future ground stops would be announced alongside a pre-printed list of non-causes, and that the router had been thanked for its service and quietly moved to a drawer marked 'definitely fine'.
